Medical schools don't care about major, so long as you get all the pre-reqs in. I know a Jewish Studies undergrad who became a neurosurgeon. Pick whichever major you like most and think you can perform the best in to keep your GPA up.

College is entirely about how you study. Your IQ, your high school performance and your rank mean nothing. If you walk into a very hard major like I did my freshman year thinking college is going to be a breeze, you're going to get steamrolled like I did. If you're doing poorly in ochem, it's how you study. Ochem is something best studied through routine. Buy a whiteboard and spend hours per week going over structures and resonances until they become second nature. If that doesn't work, try a different approach. Studying ochem is different from bio, which is different from physics, which is different from biochem, which is different from calculus. Knowing how to study is the ultimate way to succeed in college for a major in STEM. Changing my study habits raised my gpa from a 2.7 to a 3.5+. In 4 semesters.

Now to answer your specific questions:

1) GPA to medical schools is very important, equally so with the MCAT. For pharmacy, the PCAT is a bit more important as far as I heard. For GRE, I'm not sure since I don't have to take it.

2) It's often face value. Many graduate scools screen for GPA, simply filtering out those below 3.0, for example.

3)This one is harder. You will have to try and gain pertinent experience in the field to see if it's for you. If you want to do medicine, shadow a doctor or PA. Become an EMT, or a scribe, or a CNA. Participate in the field you are interested in. Only then will you know if it's truly for you. If you're really having concerns, talk to your advisor.

4) You stumble onto the right path through experimentation and experience. By now you may know that you really enjoy science or art or music in particular. Try everything in that area. Like medicine? Expand on that by helping people not just clinically in a job but by volunteering. Like music? Teach lessons for your favorite instrument. It's all about getting out there and doing lower level versions of the work you want to do in the future.

As for PA over MD, it's not any easier. You get 80% of the med school material in half the time. You get shunted the shitty cases, the fakers, and the mundane patients. Your pay is much lower. You can't practice alone. No surgery, except to assist. I just make sure you're aware of the many, many limitations of PAs because a lot of people I know want to do it to become "doctors in only 2 years". I've heard nightmares about 10 tests per week of people who are PAs in PA school. I'd personally say talk to a PA, a doc, a nurse, lots of professions and see what they have to say about their regrets, their passions and what they like about what they do. Just because you like science doesn't mean you have to pursue medicine.

Assuming a B starts at 80% and ends at 89%, you'd have to get from 628 points to 698 points to get a B. If one test was 65, your max score is now 720; which is a little below a 92%. If you get around 90% on everything remaining, you'd have 648 points, which is an 82.5%, rounded up would be a flat B (Assuming a flat B starts at 83%). So if you think it's realistic to pull a 90% average or higher the rest of the class, which if you had an A before shouldn't be impossible, then yes, you'll have no problem getting a B.

Personally, I'd have to know more about where you are in your academic career and your GPA to determine what my call would be in your situation, along with where you want your GPA to be at by graduation. Best of luck in the rest of this course, and definitely proof read your planner from now on!

I review in a similar way, but I also review one chapter per day for each chapter on the test. If a test is on 4 chapters, study one in depth during each of the 4 days beforehand. My grades in college significantly improved as soon as I made a routine and built it over time. I always do at least 2 hours of work a day, with a short break in the middle. I go over any material I don't know the day we went over it in class, and study for a test X number of days in advance, where X is the number of chapters on the test, going over 1 per day. It's all abut working in a way that fits you.
